notice: framework pointers for research. verify every authority and its current treatment before citing.

signals.label: Deliberate ignorance (ostrich)
signals.description: Someone saw a high probability of a problem and took deliberate steps not to confirm it. Global-Tech: (1) subjective belief of high probability, (2) deliberate action to avoid learning.

avoidance: kept (?:himself|herself|themselves) (?:in the dark|uninformed|out of the loop)

prototypes: The CEO told staff he did not want to know about the audit findings.
After the whistleblower complaint the CFO stopped attending the meetings where the problems were discussed.
She instructed her team not to put the concerns in writing so she would not be told.
He deliberately avoided reading the internal reports that warned of the defects.
The executives turned a blind eye to red flags and never asked any follow-up questions.
Defendants consciously avoided confirming what they strongly suspected was true.
questions: Who held the suspicion, and what made the probability high?
What specific act shows avoidance rather than mere inattention?
Is there a date tying the avoidance to the warning?

authorities.label: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754 (2011)

signals.label: Red flags ignored
signals.description: Warnings reached the defendant and nothing was done. Recklessness via ignoring reasonably available information or failing to check information there was a duty to monitor.
prototypes: The audit committee was warned about the revenue practices and took no action.
Management ignored repeated complaints from customers about the defective product.
Despite the internal audit finding, the CFO failed to investigate the discrepancy.
Executives dismissed the engineers' concerns and kept shipping.
questions: What exactly was the warning and who received it?
When did it arrive relative to the challenged statement?
What would a reasonable follow-up have revealed?

authorities.label: Novak v. Kasaks, 216 F.3d 300 (2d Cir. 2000)
authorities.point: recklessness through ignoring reasonably available data

authorities.label: In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig., 183 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 1999)

signals.label: Contrary internal information
signals.description: Internal reports, data or meetings showed the opposite of what was said publicly at the time it was said.
prototypes: Weekly sales reports sent to the CEO showed demand collapsing while he told analysts demand was strong.
Internal dashboards reflected the backlog decline at the time the company reaffirmed guidance.
Board materials showed the defect rate rising even as the press release touted product quality.
questions: Which document, what date, who received it?
Does the document contradict the specific statement or just the general topic?

authorities.label: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007)

signals.label: Reassurance after warning
signals.description: Public reassurance that came after the speaker had been warned. Ordering matters: the warning has to come first.
prototypes: Even after receiving the auditor's warning, the CFO continued to assure investors the numbers were sound.
Despite being told about the safety defect, the CEO nonetheless told analysts there were no quality issues.
questions: Can the warning and the statement both be dated?
Was the statement about the same subject the warning covered?

authorities.label: Novak v. Kasaks, 216 F.3d 300 (2d Cir. 2000)
authorities.point: statements made despite knowledge of contrary facts

signals.label: Suspicious trading timing
signals.description: Insider sales close in time to undisclosed bad news. Courts look at amount, percentage of holdings, timing, and consistency with prior trading.
prototypes: The CFO sold 70 percent of his holdings two weeks before the company disclosed the restatement.
Insiders unloaded millions of dollars of stock shortly before the corrective disclosure.
The sales were unusual in amount and timing compared with the executive's prior trading.
questions: What share of holdings was sold, and what was the prior baseline?
Was there a pre-existing 10b5-1 plan?
Did other insiders sell or hold?

authorities.label: In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig., 183 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 1999)
Acito v. IMCERA Grp., Inc., 47 F.3d 47 (2d Cir. 1995)
Metzler Inv. GMBH v. Corinthian Colls., Inc., 540 F.3d 1049 (9th Cir. 2008)

signals.label: 10b5-1 plan timing
signals.description: A trading plan adopted, changed or cancelled close to bad news or to the trades it covers. Since the 2022 amendments officers face a cooling-off period before trading under a new or modified plan.

temporal.note: plan change to first trade under 90 days, check the cooling-off rules that applied on that date

prototypes: The CEO adopted a 10b5-1 plan three weeks before the announcement and began selling under it immediately.
Executives modified their trading plans days before the company cut guidance.
questions: Adoption or modification date versus first trade date?
Was the plan adopted while the insider was aware of the undisclosed problem?

signals.label: Executive departure timing
signals.description: A senior officer leaves around the time the problem comes out. Departures alone are weak; timing plus a link to the misconduct is what counts.
prototypes: The CFO abruptly resigned two weeks before the company announced the restatement.
The controller was terminated days after the internal investigation began.
questions: Stated reason for leaving?
What sourced fact links the departure to the misconduct?

authorities.label: Zucco Partners, LLC v. Digimarc Corp., 552 F.3d 981 (9th Cir. 2009)

signals.label: Auditor / gatekeeper exit
signals.description: Auditor resignation, withdrawn opinion, disagreement, or a disclosed material weakness.
prototypes: The outside auditor resigned and withdrew its opinion on the prior financial statements.
The company disclosed a material weakness in internal controls over revenue recognition.
questions: What did the auditor say on the way out?
Was the weakness tied to the accounts at issue?

signals.label: Concealment / consciousness of guilt
signals.description: Steps to hide information: deleted records, off-system communications, side letters, misleading auditors.
prototypes: The CFO told the controller not to put anything in writing and to use his personal phone.
Executives deleted the emails discussing the problem after the subpoena arrived.
Side letters granting return rights were hidden from the auditors.
questions: Who did it, when, and what was hidden?
Is there a document or witness for the act itself?

signals.label: Concrete personal motive
signals.description: A specific personal benefit tied to the fraud. Generic motives every executive shares (high stock price, bonuses) are usually not enough in the Second Circuit.
prototypes: The CEO's bonus was tied to hitting the quarterly revenue target he announced.
Defendants needed the inflated stock price to close the acquisition paid for in shares.
The founder had pledged his shares and faced a margin call if the price fell.
questions: Is the benefit personal to the defendant and unusual, or shared by all executives?
Did the defendant actually realize it?

authorities.label: ECA & Local 134 IBEW Joint Pension Tr. v. JP Morgan Chase Co., 553 F.3d 187 (2d Cir. 2009)
authorities.point: motive must be concrete and personal

signals.label: Quarter-end manipulation
signals.description: Channel stuffing, pull-ins, bill-and-hold, round-trips, or other end-of-period moves to hit a number.
prototypes: In the last days of each quarter the sales team shipped product early with extended payment terms to hit guidance.
Revenue was pulled forward from the next quarter through bill-and-hold arrangements.
questions: Which quarters and how much revenue?
Who directed it?

signals.label: SOX certification with red flags
signals.description: An officer signed a SOX 302/906 certification while red flags were present. Certification alone is generally not scienter; it matters when paired with glaring warnings.
prototypes: The CFO signed SOX certifications attesting to internal controls weeks after the controller warned him about the reserve manipulation.
questions: What warning did the signer have before signing?

authorities.label: Zucco Partners, LLC v. Digimarc Corp., 552 F.3d 981 (9th Cir. 2009)
authorities.point: certifications need knowledge of the problem

statutes.label: Exchange Act § 10(b) / Rule 10b-5
statutes.standard: Intent to deceive, manipulate or defraud, or recklessness. PSLRA requires particular facts giving a strong inference, at least as compelling as any opposing inference.

circuits.2: Motive and opportunity, or strong circumstantial evidence of conscious misbehavior or recklessness.
circuits.9: Deliberate recklessness; allegations reviewed holistically, core operations inference is narrow.

authorities: Tellabs, Inc. v. Makor Issues & Rights, Ltd., 551 U.S. 308 (2007)
In re Silicon Graphics Inc. Sec. Litig., 183 F.3d 970 (9th Cir. 1999)
South Ferry LP, #2 v. Killinger, 542 F.3d 776 (9th Cir. 2008)

statutes.label: Insider trading under Rule 10b-5 / 10b5-1
statutes.standard: Trading on the basis of material nonpublic information, meaning aware of it when trading. Qualifying 10b5-1 plans are an affirmative defense; amended plan conditions apply to plans adopted or modified after the 2023 effective date.

statutes.label: Securities Act § 11
statutes.standard: No scienter needed; issuer strictly liable, others have a due diligence defense. Intent signals matter only if the claim sounds in fraud, which pulls in Rule 9(b) particularity.

circuits.2: Rule 9(b) applies to § 11 claims premised on fraud.
circuits.9: Rule 9(b) applies to § 11 claims that sound in fraud.

authorities: Rubke v. Capitol Bancorp Ltd., 551 F.3d 1156 (9th Cir. 2009)

statutes.label: Securities Act § 12(a)(2)
statutes.standard: No scienter; defendant can show it did not know and could not have known with reasonable care. Same 9(b) caveat as § 11 if pleaded as fraud.

statutes.label: Exchange Act § 14(a) / Rule 14a-9
statutes.standard: Negligence is generally enough for proxy claims. Check circuit authority for the defendant type.
authorities: Gerstle v. Gamble-Skogmo, Inc., 478 F.2d 1281 (2d Cir. 1973)

statutes.label: Securities Act § 17(a) (SEC)
statutes.standard: § 17(a)(1) requires scienter; § 17(a)(2) and (3) need only negligence. No private right of action.

statutes.label: Exchange Act § 20(a) control person
statutes.standard: Needs a primary violation plus control. Second Circuit adds culpable participation; Ninth Circuit does not, but allows a good faith defense.

circuits.9: No culpable participation element; good faith defense.

authorities: ATSI Commc'ns, Inc. v. Shaar Fund, Ltd., 493 F.3d 87 (2d Cir. 2007)
Howard v. Everex Sys., Inc., 228 F.3d 1057 (9th Cir. 2000)

statutes.label: Exchange Act § 9 manipulation
statutes.standard: Willful conduct with a manipulative purpose, such as inducing others to trade.

statutes.label: Exchange Act § 16(b) short-swing
statutes.standard: Strict liability. Intent and timing signals do not matter to liability.

statutes.label: SOX § 304 clawback
statutes.standard: Reimbursement does not require personal misconduct by the CEO or CFO.

statutes.label: Criminal securities fraud (15 U.S.C. § 78ff)
statutes.standard: Willfully. Conscious avoidance can substitute for actual knowledge under the Global-Tech test.
authorities: Global-Tech Appliances, Inc. v. SEB S.A., 563 U.S. 754 (2011)
